Breaking: The 8 Best Slippers for Women for Max Coziness, Tested By a Style Writer

📅 09 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Now that the weather has cooled down and leaves are on the ground, my style writer brain is in peak outfit mode.
  • According to recent reports, A lot of the same principles that apply to shopping for supportive sneakers also apply to slippers, says Anne Sharkey, DPM, a podiatrist at Solely Podiatry in Austin, TX.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Now that the weather has cooled down and leaves are on the ground, my style writer brain is in peak outfit mode. I’ve already imagined the ways I’ll wear my leather jackets, chunky knits, and bootcut jeans. But before I start styling my way through the fall and winter, there’s one essential I always reach for first: slippers. I test a lot of shoes in the name of journalism, and few spark more joy than a pair of cute slippers that add the perfect cozy feel to any outfit. Whether I’m channeling my inner couch potato on a lazy Sunday or running errands around town, the best slippers in my stash hit the sweet spot of soft, supportive, and actually stylish.

According to recent reports, A lot of the same principles that apply to shopping for supportive sneakers also apply to slippers, says Anne Sharkey, DPM, a podiatrist at Solely Podiatry in Austin, TX. After all, a slipper is the ultimate cozy shoe, but it’s also incredibly useful for keeping your arches happy while walking around hardwood floors at home. That’s why Sharkey says cushioning and arch support are key. Your slippers should feel plush underfoot, but not so squishy that you lose stability. Where you proposal to wear them also matters: A pair of house slippers needs less traction and durability than a pair for outdoors, which should have a thicker, more grippy bottom.

After over a year of testing, I found slippers that are plush enough to lounge in, supportive enough for a spin around town, and stylish enough that you’ll actually want to wear them.

When it comes to a slipper that checks every box (plush, supportive, and legitimately stylish), the Ugg Cozy Slipper is the one I always come back to. I’ve been wearing this slipper since fall 2024 with everything from jeans and Henleys to matching sweat sets.

The slipper earns its name with extra-cozy materials, from the sheepskin fur lining to the sweater-knit outer and fluffy collar. I love that it keeps my feet warm and toasty, even during cold winter months. Board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bobby Pourizaee, DPM says this slipper is excellent for comfort and lounging. Podiatrist and board-certified foot and ankle surgeon Bruce Pinker, DPM agrees, adding that the slip-on style makes this slipper easy to wear.

Industry observers note that beneath the fluff, there’s real structure that keeps my feet fatigue-free. The contoured footbed and firm-yet-plush midsole made with 17 mm of sheepskin hug my arches just right. The outsole is sturdy and grippy, made with dense EVA foam and tons of traction. I wear it on long walks with my dog around the Long Island suburbs and never worry about slipping or falling, no matter the weather. However, it’s still lightweight enough to feel like an indoor slipper.

Pinker says that it could be improved if the heel region were closed for more support and stability, but the easy-on, easy-off fit is part of why I love this slipper. If you’re after something warm, cozy, and super stylish for both indoor and outdoor wear, I can’t recommend this slipper enough.

Read More: Ugg Cozy Slipper Review.

It has been revealed that for a cozy, budget-friendly slipper that doesn’t skimp on comfort, the Dearfoams Lacey Memory Foam Slipper is the one I’ve been living in lately. At under $30, this slipper is way more cushy, warm, and supportive than lots of other house slippers I’ve worn.

Sources indicate that I padded around my house in this slipper nonstop for about a year, and it held up beautifully through coffee runs to the kitchen, long hours at my desk, and quick trips to grab packages. It’s definitely a house slipper, but in the best way possible—pure comfort, with just enough structure to feel supportive.

Industry observers note that the memory foam cushioning is what makes this slipper so comfortable, Sharkey says. Each step in it feels super plush, molding to the shape of my foot for that “walking on pillows” feel. The fleece lining also keeps my feet cozy without overheating, and the soft knit upper gives it a lounge-all-day kind of vibe that pairs perfectly with pajamas and sweatpants. I absolutely love the heel and arch cushioning, especially when my feet ache after a long day commuting to and from Manhattan, but Sharkey says they should only be worn in the house since they lack the structure needed for long periods on your feet.

But for a house slipper, there’s way more support than I expected. The raised heel area keeps the slipper from sliding off my foot, even when I’m walking up or down stairs. It’s a small but thoughtful feature that makes it feel a bit more secure than your average slip-on. And while the outsole isn’t meant for outdoor adventures, it’s durable enough for quick steps onto the porch or grabbing the mail.

I wore this slipper for nearly a year straight while trodding around my house, and absolutely love them. However, I will say that at about the 10-month mark, they needed to be replaced, as they stretched out a bit and lost some of the much-needed cushioning, support, and traction.

Read More: Best Winter Boots For Women.

Sources indicate that thanks to its incredible level of cushioning, the Vionic Gemma II Mule Slipper keeps my feet pain-free even after walking in it all day. Pourizaee states it's a strong recommendation thanks to the contoured footbed. The midsole is made from a flexible EVA foam that not only feels super plush under my foot but is designed to absorb shock and reduce stress on the joints. I have lingering ankle and foot pain on one side from a previous high ankle sprain, and while some shoes exacerbate those symptoms, this slipper keeps my feet happy. That comes as no surprise, since this slipper earned an APMA Seal of Acceptance.

It has been revealed that it also has great support and stability features. Pinker says it would be improved with a closed-heel design, but I find that the deep heel cup helps, and the strap closure keeps my foot firmly planted—even while speed walking on city sidewalks. Pourizaee adds that the contoured footbed helps keep feet aligned and relieves foot strain. While I often wake up with sore feet that hurt as soon as I step out of bed, I find that when I’ve worn this slipper the day before, foot fatigue is next to zero.

In a recent development, if you like a cozy slipper, the Gemma II delivers. I have the cream color, which is made with a wool upper that keeps my feet warm and looks cute with all my cold-weather loungewear. Other styles have a faux-fur or flannel upper, which also looks super warm and cozy. Plus, since the slipper is designed for indoor and outdoor wear, the synthetic outsole is ultra-durable with a patterned tread design. I’ve even gone for post-rain walks with my dog on wet pavement, and never felt like I was going to slip.

Overall, this slipper is warm, cozy, and ultra-cushioned. It keeps my feet happy with the plush feel underfoot, and I love keeping it by the door when I need a cute shoe to slip on fast.

If you need a slipper with serious arch support, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper delivers. Plus, it comes with additional insoles and spacers for days when my feet need extra support.

The Ortho-Cushion system (which includes the removable orthotic insole, ergonomic sole, and fitting spacers) helps to customize the fit and level of cushioning and support. I didn’t realize before selecting my normal size that Orthofeet recommends ordering a half-size down for a more snug fit, but placing the smallest blue fitting spacer (1/16 inch) under the insole kept my foot feeling super secure. Even without any customization, I was impressed by the high level of cushioning that hugs my arches and feels really nice under my heels. The ergonomic sole not only has ample cushioning underfoot, but also the subtle “rocker” design, which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to a rocking chair. That shape propels you forward with each step and also helps take some pressure off the joints. Plus, the EVA outsole also has lots of traction patterns to keep every step feeling stable and secure.

Recent findings suggest that I also love the faux fur lining and insole that feels super cozy and keeps my feet warm even while walking outdoors on chilly mornings. The suede outer adds to that cozy vibe and looks super cute. I initially wasn’t sure if this slipper would be my style, but I find myself reaching for it all the time when I leave the house for quick errands and coffee dates with friends. I have the taupe color and often pair it with ankle jeans and sweaters for a comfortable fall fit.

In a recent development, while it does run slightly small, the brand offers half sizes, and the slipper comes with customizable features, so I didn’t find it an glitch at all. However, if you’re concerned about fit, I recommend ordering a half size down.

The Sunday Mule Slipper from Bombas is perhaps the most stylish casual shoe that I own. The elongated, oval-toe shape looks super chic, and it's wrapped entirely in a fluffy sherpa material for that cozy-yet-put-together feel. Whether I’m couch-rotting on the weekend, grabbing a latte, or taking a casual stroll around town, I can always count on this slipper. It looks great with a wide-leg lounge pant or leggings with slouchy socks, but I’ve also worn it with a cropped pair of jeans.

Sharkey states it's a good cozy and comfortable option, and that Bombas did a great job with the level of cushioning. That’s thanks to the memory foam footbed, which has a nice squishy feel, contours to the shape of the foot, and softens impact with every step. That contouring feature does wonders for making sure the slipper stays on, even while trekking all around town. However, Sharkey says the backless design does tend to slip off the feet if you’re not careful. I haven’t had any complications there, but it’s something to keep in mind if your feet need an ultra-supportive shoe—in which case, the Orthofeet Charlotte Slipper might be a better choice.

Sources indicate that the rubber outsole gives this slip-on shoe a major upgrade, since it helps provide traction when I wear it outside. I keep this slipper mainly for wearing around the house or quick errands, but I have worn it during short, casual walks without worry. The fluffy sherpa material, inside and out, makes it a super cozy option for lazy days cuddled up on the couch and keeps my feet warm even when I take it for a spin outdoors.

Plus, there’s plenty of chic color options. I went with the cream, which I find pairs well with almost anything in my closet—but there’s also a black and brown for additional neutrals, and a dusty purple or tomato red option for something more bold. While this slipper from Bombas might not be the most supportive option, I’d recommend it to anyone looking for a plush, super stylish slipper.

Industry observers note that clogs get a bad rap for making your feet sweat, slide around, and (sorry!) being kind of ugly. But this slip-on clog from Rothy’s nails it on the style front, and is also durable, breathable, and super comfortable. The Casual Clog is well-loved by me and executive editor Abigail Cuffey—oh, and Sharkey recommends it, too.

This slipper/clog hybrid is made with the brand’s signature cushioning made from recycled water bottles and arch support that Sharkey states is ultra comfortable. She also says she likes that the heel cup is a bit deeper than your standard slipper, which helps with stability. I find that the deep heel cup helps cover the back of my foot, so it doesn’t slip off when I’m running around the house doing laundry or walking up and down stairs. The outsole is also made from recycled water bottles and has a grooved design that makes it super durable with tons of traction. I usually wear it for casual outings and meeting up with friends, and find it looks great with baggy jeans and sweaters for a casual-yet-put-together look.

While I own the merino wool version, Cuffey owns both the merino wool and hemp styles. She’s been wearing the hemp clog since fall 2024, and loves that the ultra-cushioned footbed molds to her feet. “It feels like a hug for your heels and toes,” she notes. She wears it as a lounge shoe and an outdoor shoe, because of the grippy outsole and substantial feel. Cuffey’s thoughts on the merino wool clog are generally the same, but she loves that the wool feels a little cozier while still airy and breathable. “I usually go through slippers so fast because they get so gross, but Rothy’s Casual Clogs are the first ones that have staying power in my closet,” she says.

In a recent development, it does run a little wide, but the fabric is stretchy, so I haven’t had any issues with it feeling too loose on my feet. But if you’re in between sizes, Rothy’s recommends sizing down for a better fit.

According to recent reports, the L.L. Bean Wicked Good Moccasin has become my favorite ever since I got it in the mail. A moccasin is a slipper made of soft leather that wraps around the foot with a single gathered seam at the front. This style is the cushiest, coziest, most supportive I’ve ever worn, earning a permanent spot in my fall and winter footwear rotation.

Unlike some moccasins, Pinker says this style feels especially stable thanks to the rubber outsole with added grip and traction. Plus, the suede material is more structured than other moccasins I’ve worn, which makes for a snug, secure feel. I’ve worn this moccasin weekly over the past month, and I can tell it’s extremely durable. The suede has a lot of heft, and combined with the hand-stitched construction, this moccasin stands up to wear and tear. The fur lining is also extremely comfortable and warm, and I love wearing this shoe on colder days to keep my feet toasty. The insole is also made from the same fur material, which delivers a super plush, cushioned feel underfoot.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also plenty of fur lining the outside of the slipper, which I find super stylish, along with the rawhide laces and bow. It looks great with both joggers and wide-leg sweatpants, and I even wore it recently with cuffed jeans and a boxy sweater for a casual brunch. I have the brown pair, but with seven shades to choose from (including blue, red, and purple!), there’s no shortage of styling potential.

Industry observers note that one note: this slipper is spot-clean only, unlike others that can go in the washing machine. However, I wear it nearly every morning lately to walk my dog when the ground is still dewy, and I haven’t gotten any stains that took more than a quick pass with a dry washcloth to remove.

It has been revealed that I desperately needed a new house slipper a few weeks ago, so I decided to snag this pair from Fulton—and I couldn’t be happier with my decision. While you could totally get away with wearing this slipper outside (it’s super cute and definitely sturdy), I love keeping this pair inside and free from outside germs—IYKYK.

Industry observers note that at first, I honestly wasn’t sure this pair would be a winner: the footbed was super uncomfortable the first day that I wore them. It felt like all the raised areas were in the wrong places, which made it a little difficult to walk. Had I known then that the Fulton website explains there’s a 10-hour break-in process, I’d have been way less concerned.

In a recent development, lo and behold, by the following day the slippers felt much better—and only continued to get more comfortable as the cork footbed molded to the exact shape of my foot. I wouldn’t call this slipper plush by any means (though the wool upper is quite cozy), so if that’s what you’re looking for, the Ugg, Dearfoams, Orthofeet, or L.L. Bean styles might be better options. But this shoe makes my feet feel so good.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been suffering from some pretty gnarly foot pain from recently developed plantar fasciitis, but since I started wearing this slipper around the house every day, my feet feel brand latest. My arches and heels feel way less achy throughout the day, and it no longer hurts to plant my feet on the ground first thing in the morning.

Sources indicate that if you prefer a slide over a slipper, this pick from Oofos is perfect. I often bring it to the gym to wear in the locker room, sauna, or on the way to my post-workout smoothie spot, and the cushy foam insole feels great on my achy feet. As our WH 2025 Fitness Awards winner for Best Recovery Shoe, I had to test it myself for this guide.

Industry observers note that pourizaee claims this slide is ideal for recovery or all-day wear thanks to its excellent shock absorption and built-in arch support. That’s because it’s made from the brand's signature OOfoam technology—a springy EVA foam that has plenty of cushion and feels nice and squishy underfoot. The insole’s contoured shape creates built-in arch support, with a high mound near the center that fits perfectly under the arches. That shape reduces stress on the knees, ankles, and other joints. My ankle pain (from a previous sprain) and mysterious knee pain definitely feel better when I wear this slide regularly around the house. Plus, the deep heel cup keeps my foot anchored in place, even when I’m doing housework at lightning speed.

WH executive health and fitness director, Jacqueline Andriakos, swears by it for managing her foot pain, too. "My podiatrist told me I had to get a pair for work-from-home days and going to and from barefoot workout classes," she says. "I notice my chronic foot pain is light years better when I’ve been wearing it more regularly.".

According to recent reports, another perk? The foam is water-repellent, odor-resistant, and machine washable. The only feature that would make this slide better, Pinker indicates, is an ankle strap for extra stability and support.

The right cushioning absorbs impact from walking on hard surfaces to help prevent foot pain, notes Pourziaee. All of our favorite slippers have at least a medium level of cushioning.

Since then, I’ve continued to put the originally tested slippers through their paces, wearing some pairs on long walks with my dog around Long Island and even commuting to work in Manhattan in a few styles to see how they held up to my daily 10,000-step-count goal.

#29312. ‘Dune: Part Three’: An Exclusive First Look at the Sets

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1102 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

‘Dune: Part Three’: An Exclusive First Look at the Sets

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that nothing about the cinematic language of Dune is small—director Denis Villeneuve’s film trilogy does span multiple planets, after all.
  • “My approach has always been with symbolism and semiotics,” Vermette tells AD.
  • In conversation with Vermette about the sci-fi epic, examples of that core tenet come up often.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nothing about the cinematic language of Dune is small—director Denis Villeneuve’s film trilogy does span multiple planets, after all. But throughout his work on the movies, including the upcoming Dune: Part Three, production designer Patrice Vermette has made sure to stay focused on the little details.

“My approach has always been with symbolism and semiotics,” Vermette tells AD. “It is my philosophy of design, because for Denis, empty design cannot exist. Things need to have a purpose. Need to have a signification.”.

In conversation with Vermette about the sci-fi epic, examples of that core tenet come up often. Carefully designed details imbue hidden meaning in each set, creating a captivating, immersive on-screen world that earned the designer an Oscar for his work in the first Dune. The trilogy’s latest installment, Dune: Part Three, which lands in theaters on December 18, expands on that ethos. And for the final film in the series, the sheer scale of the sets was larger. “It was our last chance working in that world,” Vermette indicates. “It’s like in a fireworks [display], it’s the end, it’s the bouquet final, it’s like, ‘alright, let’s do it!’”.

Robert Pattinson as Scytale, with director Denis Villeneuve.

According to recent reports, over 450,000 square feet of interior stages and 475,000 square feet of backlots were used for scenes shot in Budapest alone, with each set typically taking 14 to 16 weeks to build. (Filming also took place in Abu Dhabi and Iceland.) Even the sandworms that slither through the titular dunes got grander this time around: Instead of the relatively small platforms that were used to film worm-riding sequences as in the previous films, the production team built a 300-foot-long by 65-foot-wide sandworm in the middle of the desert.

Like in Dune: Part Two, Vermette was challenged to create entirely fresh sets for this installment, which adapts Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel Dune Messiah. One of the new settings viewers can expect is Wallach IX, the home of the powerful and secretive Bene Gesserit sisterhood. Throughout their planet, Vermette incorporated stone etchings that resemble human cells seen through a microscope, referencing the Bene Gesserit’s breeding program that has gone on for millennia. Mother nature also informed the architecture. “When you arrive on the planet, the buildings are basically eggs of a spider, like crops of spider eggs as you find them in nature,” Vermette explains. “Ecology has always been a huge source of inspiration for me, and also for the storytelling it gives—you know, they’ve got their web across the universe, for the genealogy they create.”.

It has been revealed that another upcoming setting is the Veteran’s District, where the Fremen, the native inhabitants of the desert planet Arrakis, retire after fighting in the catastrophic holy war spurred by Paul Atreides, aka Muad’Dib (Timothée Chalamet). In the previous films, the Fremen lived in communal residences lined with hand-carved stone that recorded their history and culture. Returning from the battlefield, they find mass-produced housing units instead of the “green paradise” they were promised would await them. Made of ceramic instead of rock, with stamped-on rather than hand-carved markings, the Veteran’s District represents an artificial facsimile of their former homes. “And when you put all these units together, and you look at the rooftops, it’s there to represent sand dunes,” Vermette explains. “All these triangles align [to look like dunes], but it’s fake.”.

Another circular doorway represents an all-seeing eye near the lush Imperial Gardens, which illustrate Paul’s extreme wealth and control of resources—including water—on the dry planet of Arrakis.

According to recent reports, there is a green paradise on Arrakis, just not for the Fremen. Lush gardens grace the planet’s Imperial Palace, a massive inverted pyramid with a large circle cut out of it—a reimagined version of the all-seeing eye. “I got inspired by the title of the book, Messiah, and from the fact that Denis, just like Frank Herbert, wanted to make sure that Paul Atreides was not going to be seen as a hero, and it’s a tale of being cautious about messianic figures,” indicates Vermette. Similar representations of the all-seeing eye are found throughout the palace, sinisterly implying that Muad’Dib is always watching.

Industry observers note that in actuality, Muad’Dib’s personal quarters are completely isolated from the rest of the palace. His wife, Irulan (Florence Pugh), must find her way through a twisting mass of hallways to reach him. “Basically, she’s walking into the psyche of Paul,” Vermette explains. “She goes into a void, and then it’s all these mazes of one’s mind.” When we get to the end of the maze, we see that Paul’s inner sanctum resembles a humble desert camp. Not unlike the Fremen, his dwelling has been reduced to an echo of what once was. He is “living as a recluse because he doesn’t trust anybody,” Vermette explains. “He wants to go back to a place where he felt the most comfortable, which was the desert. So he recreated that space.”.

According to recent reports, “Denis really wanted that set to be the golden cage of Irulan,” Vermette says of these private chambers. “She’s married to the emperor, but she’s not free at all, she’s a prisoner.” The window is shaped similar to an infinity symbol, but is covered in metal screens. “It’s like eternity, but eternity is blocked. It’s like a cage.”.

The entrance to the maze within Muad’Dib’s inner sanctum. Vermette designed 40 maze wall panels that needed to be moved into various configurations to shoot the scene, which was filmed in less than a day. Eight people were each assigned a portion of the 12-foot-high panels and learned a choreography of sorts, quickly moving into each configuration until they could do each one in five minutes or less. “We rehearsed and rehearsed, just like dancers or musicians; they knew exactly where to fit their pieces” within the roughly 14,400-square-foot space, indicates Vermette.

On the planet Wallach IX, the office of Bene Gesserit Reverend Mother Mohaim features stone carvings inspired by human cells under a microscope.

Recent findings suggest that the Imperial Palace throne room took 20 weeks to build. Behind Muad’Dib’s emerald throne, the windows are shielded with metal cast screens inspired by Montreal’s Saint-Ambrose Church, which was built in 1925 by architect Ernest Cormier.

The all-seeing eye is a repeating symbol Vermette inserted throughout the Imperial Palace, including a representation seen here as the circular entrance of Paul’s Keep.

The architecture of this Imperial Palace corridor has slanted walls to reflect a pyramid-shaped exterior and flying buttress support structures inspired by Gothic-style cathedrals.

#29308. The 60 Best New Highlights of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

📅 13 Feb 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2377 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

The 60 Best New Highlights of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

📅 13 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days.
  • Recent findings suggest that but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong.
  • It has been revealed that look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a significant way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

Recent findings suggest that but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even demonstrates we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

It has been revealed that look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the indicates we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

In a recent development, netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (HBO).

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock).

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

According to recent reports, the latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

According to recent reports, this wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The latest season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best demonstrates of the year.

Sources indicate that the second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

According to recent reports, one of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

In a recent development, the erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting upcoming indicates. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

In a recent development, from the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

In a recent development, there are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

In a recent development, sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

According to recent reports, this series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

Jury Duty: Company Retreat (Prime Video).

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix).

Industry observers note that camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Breaking Bad” actor and disability advocate RJ Mitte has died at age 34.

Sources indicate that mitte reportedly died by suicide, his representative told People on October 12. However, local authorities have noted the official cause and manner of his death remain under investigation.

It has been revealed that mitte, who was best-known for playing Walter White Jr. on the Emmy Award-winning television series “Breaking Bad,” lived with cerebral palsy and advocated for disability inclusion.

It has been revealed that there is currently no evidence to suggest that cerebral palsy caused the actor’s death. Still, Mitte’s untimely passing highlights the mental health challenges that people with cerebral palsy may face.

Research has demonstrated elevated risks of anxiety and depression among those with the condition, alongside barriers to diagnosis, social participation, and employment.

“Living with cerebral palsy can affect mental health through several interacting pathways,” said Shannel Elhelou, neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Centric Neuropsychology in Westlake Village, CA.

“Chronic pain, fatigue, disrupted sleep, and the effort required to navigate daily activities can take an emotional toll. Experiences of bullying, discrimination, social exclusion, and difficulty accessing care can add to that burden. Also, the early brain injury underlying cerebral palsy may contribute to difficulties with emotional regulation, although each person’s experience is different,” Elhelou told Healthline.

If you or someone you know is in crisis and considering suicide or self-harm, please seek support:.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re calling on behalf of someone else, stay with them until help arrives. You may remove weapons or substances that can cause harm if you can do so safely.

If you’re not in the same household, stay on the phone with them until help arrives.

Mitte played a key role in challenging stereotypes by portraying a teenager with cerebral palsy on “Breaking Bad.”.

Outside of acting, Mitte advocated for people with disabilities through organizations including United Cerebral Palsy (UCP) and Shriners Children’s.

He also led the Mitte Foundation, a non-profit corporation founded in 1994 by his grandparents, Roy F. and Joann Cole Mitte, that improves the quality of life for people in Central Texas.

Mitte’s advocacy emphasized representation, inclusion, and opportunities for people with disabilities.

The legacy he leaves behind underscores the need to recognize mental health as an essential part of care for individuals with cerebral palsy and other disabilities.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of conditions affecting movement, posture, and coordination.

Most people with cerebral palsy have typical intelligence, although some also have intellectual disabilities or other comorbid physical and mental health conditions.

A 2018 study published in JAMA Neurology found that adults with cerebral palsy had a 28% higher risk of developing depression and a 40% higher risk of anxiety than adults without the condition.

A 2024 study in JAMA Network Open found higher recorded rates of anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) among children and young adults with cerebral palsy.

The researchers also identified comparatively low rates of depression and suicidal ideation, highlighting concerns that these conditions may be underdiagnosed.

“Research reveals that adults with cerebral palsy have an increased risk of depression and anxiety,” Elhelou noted.

Sources indicate that “However, these conditions should never be viewed as an inevitable part of having a disability. One concern is ‘diagnostic overshadowing,’ when symptoms of depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions are attributed to cerebral palsy itself, leading those conditions to go unrecognized and untreated. Someone’s fatigue, withdrawal, or changes in behavior deserve careful assessment rather than the assumption that ‘this is just their cerebral palsy,'” she continued.

It has been revealed that “While these findings help us understand mental health risks among people with cerebral palsy, they cannot tell us what any one person was experiencing. Many interacting factors may contribute to someone dying by suicide, and it would be inappropriate to attribute an individual’s death to their disability.”.

A 2019 study published in Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology found that children with cerebral palsy had higher odds of anxiety disorders and behavioral challenges than children without the condition.

Difficulties with friendships and bullying were associated with some of these differences.

Factors that may affect well-being include:.

The researchers also found that supportive friendships may help reduce some of these disparities, reinforcing the importance of inclusive schools and communities.

A 2021 study published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine found that U.S. adults with disabilities faced increased risks of suicidal thoughts, planning, and attempts compared with adults without disabilities.

The 988 Lifeline received more than 8 million contacts through calls, texts, chats, and American Sign Language videophone in 2025, according to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration.

Federal funding for the Lifeline’s dedicated LGBTQ+ youth service ended in July 2025, removing the option to press 3 for specialized support.

After pressure from Congress, the service was recently restored at the end of September, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF).

Employment and financial independence can influence well-being for anyone, particularly those with cerebral palsy.

However, a 2024 study found that just 30.4% of young adults with cerebral palsy who participated in vocational rehabilitation programs were employed when they exited those programs.

Workplace accommodations, accessible hiring, vocational rehabilitation, and inclusive social opportunities can help address these barriers.

“Depression and anxiety are treatable, and they should never be dismissed as an inevitable part of living with a disability,” Elhelou said.

It has been revealed that “If you notice persistent sadness, anxiety, hopelessness, or withdrawal, reach out to someone you trust and a mental health professional. You deserve a clinician who takes your concerns seriously and adapts treatment to your communication, mobility, or other access needs. Care should also address pain, fatigue, and sleep difficulties, which can affect emotional well-being.”.

Organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy offer information and support for people with cerebral palsy and their families.

Healthcare professionals can also improve outcomes by screening for mental health concerns, using appropriate assessment tools, and connecting patients with accessible treatment.

Improved access to care, inclusive communities, and meaningful opportunities can help people with cerebral palsy and other disabilities thrive.

Recent findings suggest that “Asking for help does not diminish your resilience or your contributions. If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide or feel overwhelmed, you do not have to wait until things feel unbearable to reach out,” Elhelou mentioned.

It has been revealed that “Supportive relationships, peer groups, and disability communities can offer connection and understanding. Staying engaged in activities that bring enjoyment and meaning can also help.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.
  • And now it has taken a significant step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it states it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a significant step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

Sources indicate that it’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, notes this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”.

Sources indicate that we’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?).

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison claims it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

#29298. Latest Update: Juiced unveils another lower-cost moto-styled electric bike: Scrambler Core

Latest Update: Juiced unveils another lower-cost moto-styled electric bike: Scrambler Core

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a newly introduced, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core.
  • The upcoming Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.
  • Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a newly introduced, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core. The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.

The upcoming Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.

Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.

Recent findings suggest that teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.

It has been revealed that the launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The organization was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a latest generation of its popular Scrambler platform.

The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.

The standard Scrambler Hardtail launched earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).

The Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.

Battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.

It has been revealed that juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.

Recent findings suggest that those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.

Even so, vital features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.

Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.

Recent findings suggest that while the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.

According to recent reports, and with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.

Sources indicate that the Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced says preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.

At $1,399, the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Toss in the strong backing from Lectric and the 3-year warranty, and it’s hard to consider much else among the competition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican stated.

In a recent development, the Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

It has been revealed that the surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they mentioned.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially unveiled week of hospitalization.

According to recent reports, on October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican mentioned.

It has not yet been unveiled whether he will require any further treatment.

According to recent reports, adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Industry observers note that lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Recent findings suggest that treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:.

Industry observers note that surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WNBA superstar Gabby Williams is proof that hard work and persistence pay off. Drafted into the league in 2018 by the Chicago Sky, the 30-year-old has been slowly building her résumé ever since—both stateside and abroad—notching her first EuroLeague championship in 2022 with Hungary’s Sopron Basket, being named a WNBA All-Star in 2025, and, finally, winning a WNBA Championship in 2026 with the Golden State Valkyries. (She was named Finals MVP too.).

Yes, 2026 has been a massive year for the forward, and she has only a couple more months to rest up before taking on her next challenge: debuting in the Unrivaled league, as part of the Miami-based Laces BC.

Industry observers note that “It's three-on-three, so you can't hide,” Gabby tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “The positive feedback that I've heard from people who have done it, [is] that the personal development side is great. Players usually go on to have great W seasons after doing Unrivaled.”.

It has been revealed that how could Gabby possibly top this past year!? We’ll have to wait to find out, but in the meantime, she opens up about finding a home with the Valkyries, keeping herself healthy and injury-free, and building a life outside of basketball.

Over the years, Gabby has earned the nickname “the French Army knife,” due not only to her dual-citizenship (her dad is American; her mom is French) but also to her versatility on the court.

Sources indicate that her role on many teams has been defined by what the team needed, whether it was creating opportunities or defending the paint. But when she went into free agency and signed with the Valkyries earlier this year, it was the first time Gabby recalls someone in the league asking what she wanted to do.

Sources indicate that “I was proud to do whatever the team needed,” Gabby states. “But it was nice to trust myself.” That trust—both in herself and from her team—has obviously paid off. Not only does Gabby say she feels more like herself than she ever has, but she has the championship (the Valkyries’ first) to show for it.

Given how little downtime Gabby takes—she often spends part of her off-season playing abroad—she’s crafted a wellness routine that prioritizes stretching, mobility, and maintenance to keep her body in peak physical condition.

And it starts first thing when she wakes up. “I'm a massive foam-roller stretcher, especially as I'm getting older,” she states. “I'll spend a good like 20, 15 minutes first thing in the morning just doing my mobility stuff so that when I come to the gym my body's awake and ready.”.

At the gym, Gabby and her trainers prioritize accessory work over big Olympic lifts, to limit the wear and tear on her body.

Industry observers note that in the off-season, Gabby shifts from a maintenance mindset to an improvement focus with her workouts. If she wants to strengthen a particular body part or movement pattern (like being more explosive) this is when she has the time and energy to do it.

Industry observers note that no matter her training regimen, Gabby ends her day much like she starts it—with recovery. She loves an epsom salt bath and can’t get enough of her Normatec compression therapy.

It might be surprising to hear a WNBA champion say “basketball is not life,” but that’s precisely Gabby’s philosophy when it comes to balancing her priorities.

“I think that's why I've been able to have so much success in basketball is because I've learned how to compartmentalize,” she says. She credits that mindset to the coaching team at the University of Connecticut, where she played in college.

“Coach said, ‘When you're on the court, I want you to be focused. I don't want you to be thinking about school. I don't want you to be thinking about your personal life. So while you're doing your other stuff, don't focus on basketball as much. Find the time for your school. When you're going out, go out, have fun.’”.

And so Gabby does just that, whether it’s solving a puzzle or picking up a fresh book. “It is just the perfect way to consume your mind with something else,” she indicates of reading. She’s even started a Valkyries book club, but it got a bit sidetracked by, of all things, the playoffs. Luckily, there’s always the 2027 season to start anew.

To hear more from Gabby, including her undying love of figure skating and how she’s upped her style game, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

#29286. Tech Report: I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (840 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.
  • Industry observers note that it’s because I had my kids in waves.
  • There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

Industry observers note that it’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

Recent findings suggest that but the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

It has been revealed that but it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

Sources indicate that the other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.).

It has been revealed that so when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

Recent findings suggest that and there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.
