#29285. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

📅 15 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1354 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a latest study.
  • Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.
  • Industry observers note that they mentioned their findings are crucial because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a latest study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

Industry observers note that they mentioned their findings are crucial because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

It has been revealed that “We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”.

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

Industry observers note that “Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”.

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

According to recent reports, the participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

Sources indicate that however, they stated their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”.

Industry observers note that “The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”.

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”.

Recent findings suggest that shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”.

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

Sources indicate that the incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:.

In a recent development, diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi noted genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Sources indicate that colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he mentioned. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”.

#29278. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1367 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that breast cancer awareness has never been higher.
  • Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.
  • But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

In a recent development, I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

In a recent development, “It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she stated. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

Recent findings suggest that “Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

It has been revealed that for most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

It has been revealed that that aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”.

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she stated patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”.

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she mentioned: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”.

In a recent development, understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she stated. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”.

Industry observers note that for Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from newly introduced ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”.

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”.

In a recent development, “You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”.

It has been revealed that some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey reveals that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she remarked, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Weiss indicates the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and key, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”.

Recent findings suggest that peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and mentioned that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:.

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”.

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”.

Industry observers note that her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she notes she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”.

According to recent reports, “Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”.

Sources indicate that if breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

Garmin and Waze just teamed up on a clever newly introduced way to keep cyclists safer

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.
  • According to recent reports, the new feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature.
  • As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.

According to recent reports, the new feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.

As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.

I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.

According to recent reports, that’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a big difference.

In a recent development, of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.

But I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.

Industry observers note that the feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin says location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Substantial Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.

It has been revealed that this is cool but requires both a Garmin product and the Waze app. IMHO better to equip newly introduced cars and trucks with bicycle and pedestrian detection.

It has been revealed that garmin LiveTrack itself is free for owners with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.

There’s obviously one substantial limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.

But with Waze claiming around 200 million owners globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.

Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

The 10 Best Sports Bras, Tested by Fitness and Style Editors

📅 13 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3359 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

  • To find the best of the best sports bras, our fitness and style editors tested more than 50 options—from high-impact sports bras designed to minimize bounce to softer options from our fave activewear brands that prioritize comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Finding the right sports bra is crucial. That’s because a well-fitted one keeps your girls locked in and comfortable during jogs, stretches, and squats, so you don’t have to worry about spillage or bounce.

To find the best of the best sports bras, our fitness and style editors tested more than 50 options—from high-impact sports bras designed to minimize bounce to softer options from our fave activewear brands that prioritize comfort. We evaluated each pick for support, fit, comfort, and performance across a range of workouts and body types.

Read more: Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank Review.

It has been revealed that this bra is a 2026 Fitness Awards winner, and basically “the holy grail of sports bras for high-intensity workouts,” notes executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos. It’s ultra-comfortable with adjustable straps for a customizable fit that works for all sorts of exercises.

According to recent reports, the Performance Flex Bra offers medium support, but we’ve found it minimizes bounce without restricting movement, thanks to a higher neckline and light built-in padding that helps me feel secure while I train. In testing, it felt just as comfortable during slower sessions like yoga and Pilates as it did during higher-intensity workout classes. The hold is supportive without feeling overly compressive, so the girls stay in place without that squeezed-in feeling some medium-support bras can have.

Recent findings suggest that one of our favorite details is the padding. “It’s built in—so you never have to deal with shifting, scrunching, or fishing pads out of the laundry,” Andriakos states. That means the bra keeps its shape wash after wash and eliminates the annoyance of removable inserts. The padding also stays comfortable through body changes—Andriakos says it even supported her during pregnancy and postpartum. The only potential downside is that the padding isn’t removable, which might not appeal to those who want less coverage.

It has been revealed that the wide adjustable straps are another favorite feature of mine. They distribute weight evenly across my shoulders without digging in or creating pressure points during longer workouts. Even better, the straps adjust from the front, so it’s way easier to adjust than traditional bras.

And for my sweaty gals, the fabric is perfect for keeping perspiration under control. It’s made from a breathable, sweat-wicking blend of recycled polyester and elastane, which feels soft and flexible while maintaining shape. It keeps me cool and comfortable—even in heated classes—and the full mesh racerback panel adds tons of ventilation. That open, breathable design helps release heat during workouts. It also gives the bra a streamlined silhouette that sits smoothly under all my workout tops.

Read More: On Performance Flex Bra Review.

Industry observers note that this bra is a favorite among four (!) WH editors—myself, Andriakos, Wohlner, and Lauture. We love its support during high-impact workouts, durability, value, and stay-in-place cups that move like a second skin.

Andriakos says that this bra is great for medium-sized busts. It has a slight compressed feel, which keeps everything secure and minimizes bounce during plyometric moves and running, but it’s not so tight that it restricts movement. It also has a high support option, which has more compression and an adjustable band, and a low-support option, which is looser with gentle hold. We picked the medium support bra for our number one choice because it’s the most versatile option. We’ve worn it during runs, pilates, walks, yoga, and HIIT and found that it offers solid support with minimal boob bounce, but it’s not too tight that we want to rip it off after our workouts.This bra is also moisture-wicking, so it doesn’t get super wet and sweaty during workouts, which we appreciate. The 100 percent polyester material has a super slippery feel, which we like for its ability to stay breathable, but we find that it tends to chafe under the breasts during long runs. I wore this bra a ton during my half-marathon training last year and found that it would irritate my skin after about five miles. I found the solution to be to level up to the high-impact bra for my runs, so there’s less room for movement and chafing.Back to the pros: This bra handles the wash super well. Every time we wash and air dry it, the bra comes out looking good as fresh and never pills or comes unsewn. Andriakos has owned hers for two years and says it still looks the same as when she first bought it. Since then, she’s purchased multiple in different colors.“My ideal sports bra doesn’t have any hardware or fastening, or removable pads that get lost in the dryer,” says Andriakos. This one easily pulls on over the head without any adjusting and it’s a breeze to take on and off. It has a minimal silhouette with super wide armholes, so you can rip it right off after a workout without playing around with straps or closures. Plus, style contributor Ros Lauture and I love that the cups are sewn in place, so they don’t move around during your workout.

Read More: Nike Swoosh Sports Bra Review.

The first time I pulled on the Forme Power+ Bra, I instinctively rolled my shoulders forward like I usually do at my desk—except this time, they didn’t stay there. Within seconds, the bra gently guided them back, opening up my chest and lifting my upper spine so I stood noticeably taller without consciously trying. It’s a subtle shift, but one you feel immediately: less hunching, more length through your torso, and a sense that your upper body is quietly being coached into better alignment.

The Power+ is made from a compressive blend of polyester, nylon, and spandex and features multiple tension fabrics with strategically placed, double-layered support panels throughout the back and shoulders. Together, they create a gentle pull that encourages your shoulders to stay back and your chest open. The result feels supportive without restricting movement, and I love wearing it for all my workouts.

Despite its posture-focused design, the Power+ also functions as a solid sports bra. The compression keeps everything comfortably locked in during strength sessions, cardio workouts, and high-impact movement, while the breathable fabric prevents that heavy, trapped-in-sweat feeling some compressive bras create. Wide straps, generous arm openings, and a full-coverage back also help smooth things out and give the bra a flattering, secure fit.

In a recent development, another unexpected perk: It’s just as helpful during everyday wear as it is in the gym. Whether you’re sitting at a laptop for hours or driving to a workout class, the bra keeps your shoulders from rounding forward and helps reduce some of that end-of-day neck and upper-back tension I know too well.

The only downside? That supportive compression makes the bra a bit snug—especially when you’re pulling it on for the first time. And after a particularly sweaty workout, taking it off can require a little extra effort, too.

Read More: Forme Power+ Bra Review.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re a fan of Lululemon, then chances are you’ve tried this OG Energy Bra, which has been around for years. And, even after all of the brand’s launches, it remains one of our all-time favorites. Why? It’s super lightweight, breathable, sweat-wicking, soft, and it’s easy to take on and off. It slides on like a dream and feels super lightweight and comfy the whole time it’s on.

It has been revealed that “This is my go-to bra for Pilates, yoga, or barre,” indicates style contributor Kristen Saladino, who adds that it provides medium support. “The straps don't dig in and there is a good amount of coverage so when I go into downward dog I don't have to worry about my girls popping out.” She also likes that it’s suuuper stretchy, soft, and easy to take off after a sweaty workout. Plus, I find that I forget I’m even wearing it hours after I leave the gym because it’s not overly tight.

Style editor Lily Wohlner owns this bra too, and she finds it runs a bit large. Personally, she likes a tighter fit with more compression since it makes her feel more supported, so we’d recommend sizing down if you feel the same. But if you prefer a looser fit, stick with your usual size.

Industry observers note that if you need a high-impact sports bra that can handle any type of workout, this option from Under Armour will keep you locked in. According to trainers Nellie Barnett, CPT, an online fitness and wellness coach, and Taylor Beebe, a kettlebell coach and two-time USAPL (USA Powerlifting!) National Qualifier, the Infinity 2.0 High Sports Bra is the best of the best for intense workouts—no matter your chest size.

Recent findings suggest that not only do the encapsulated cups keep everything in place, but the bra is comfortable to boot. It’s still flattering, and not overly compressive (no pancake chest here!). The Infinity 2.0 also has fully adjustable straps, both in the front and back, which makes putting it on and taking it off (even after a sweaty workout) a breeze. It has a streamlined fit that’s not too tight or too loose, making it great for staying secure and moving freely during high-impact workouts. Plus, the cups have strategically placed molded padding for an aerodynamic, lightweight feel that doesn’t skimp on support. Also impressive is the bra’s moisture-wicking band that keeps underboob sweat at bay.

According to recent reports, this bra performed amazingly well during strength training, cardio, and explosive movements like burpees and high knees. It even kept Beebe feeling supported and secure throughout the entirety of a cardio kickboxing class (IYKYK). “No adjustments needed for the full hour,” she claims. If that’s not impressive, we don’t know what is.

Just be aware that the bra does run a bit small, so if you’re unsure which to pick, definitely size up.

Read More: Best Sports Bras for Large Breasts.

Industry observers note that another 2026 Fitness Awards winner for best longline sports bra, this is the rare piece that blurs the line between workout and casual clothes. The extended cut gives it the look and coverage of a cropped tank while still functioning like a supportive sports bra—making it an easy pick for everything from studio workouts to running errands.

Recent findings suggest that the versatility is exactly why it’s become a “mainstay” in associate editor Olivia Luppino’s rotation. “It’s long enough where it’s a proper top, yet also a sports bra,” she notes. “The material is thick and supportive enough, but still totally moves with you, making it functional for any workouts without compromising on style.” We also love the flattering scoop neckline, which adds a slightly elevated feel compared to more traditional sports bras.

According to recent reports, the silhouette makes it especially easy to style. You can wear it on its own with leggings or biker shorts, or layer it under an oversized tee, zip-up hoodie, or lightweight jacket. The racerback design is both flattering and functional—it allows full range of motion during workouts and sits smoothly under tanks and tees.

Performance-wise, this bra delivers high compression with medium support, offering a sculpted feel that holds the girls in place without feeling restrictive. It’s made from a sleek blend of polyester and elastane, which has a smooth, slightly shiny finish that looks super polished. The bonded (aka seamless) construction helps it lie flat and disappear under clothing, which I love when wearing beyond the gym. Another pro? The removable cups, which give you the option to customize the level of shaping and coverage.

The only caveat is that the bra is super snug. The brand recommends sizing up if you have a fuller cup size, which I agree with based on testing.

Read More: Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank Review.

This bra provides great support—we never have to worry about the girls moving out of place during wear. While this bra is made for medium impact, the cups and adjustable straps make it versatile enough for high-impact workouts. I wore it during a HIIT workout and noticed some bounce, but it’s perfect for strength training and mobility workouts that don’t involve much jumping.

Sources indicate that A lot of the high-impact sports bras we tested have hardware that digs in. That's why we love this one from Alo. When I’m in need of that extra support, the adjustable straps add more compression without digging into the skin. The removable cups can shift in the wash, but you can take them out and pop them back in for extra chest support. The one downside is that tightening the straps can put a lot of pressure on your shoulders.Plus, Lauture says this bra is one of her all-time favorites because of the fit. “It’s so flattering and it looks good on—no gaping or bunching in sight.” That’s because this bra is made with Alo’s most compressive fabric, Airlift, which offers the tightest fit of all the brand’s materials, but I found that it still has plenty of stretch that moves seamlessly even while jumping and running. With a blend of 82% polyester and 18% elastane, it’s incredibly soft, yet has a nice, tight feel to keep you supported.

Read More: Alo Airlift Suit Up Bra Review.

Recent findings suggest that A high-neck top with a built-in light support bra, this is the perfect top when you don’t feel like layering a shirt on top of a bra but you want more coverage than a bra alone. I love that this top hits at the top of my fave high-waisted leggings because it creates a seamless look. And, if you want a matching fit, it pairs perfectly with the Spacedye At Your Leisure High Waisted Midi Legging.

I like to wear this on days when I’m doing yoga, Pilates, or walking, because it provides light compression to hold the girls in place while still being comfortable enough to wear long after the gym. It’s extremely soft, as it’s made with a high polyester percentage, but the stretch comes in with the addition of elastane. I even went to brunch in this top and didn’t feel constricted at the table at all. Plus, it’s moisture-wicking to keep you dry when things start to heat up. If you’re working out outside, the shirt is treated with UV protection to protect your chest and upper waist from the sun (big ups!).

My one con: I wish that there was more coverage on the sides of the shirt to prevent the breasts from spilling out.

Recent findings suggest that the Rhone Revive Longline Bra stands out for one very specific reason: It’s actually odor-resistant. The bra is made with the brand’s specialized GoldFusion anti-odor technology, a fabric treatment that uses gold-infused particles to help tamp down on odor-causing bacteria. Whether I’m heading into hot yoga or a sweaty strength class, I appreciate that the fabric doesn’t cling to post-workout funk like others do—a small but major win.

According to recent reports, I’ve mostly worn this bra for yoga and Pilates, and it keeps everything secure, even during upside-down poses like shoulder stands (no awkward shifting or spillage, thank you!). I also wore this bra on an 85-degree day in NYC after a sweaty hot yoga class and a packed subway ride home, and somehow still felt (and smelled) fresh. I’ve never had a sports bra handle sweat this well.

It has been revealed that in terms of support, it also holds up well on short runs—but we’re not sure those with larger chests would share that experience. I mostly recommend it for low-impact workouts since the support level may not cut it for all bodies during HIIT or long runs.

I also love how easy it is to wear solo or layer under a workout tank top or t-shirt. The elastane blend is buttery soft, breathable, and moves with you. It gives just enough support without feeling overly tight or restrictive. Our only gripe? Because it’s so stretchy, you might want to size down for a snugger fit.

All in all, this bra nails comfort and performance for most workouts. Bonus points for built-in sun protection if you’re taking your workout outdoors.

If you need an ultra sweat-wicking, odor-neutralizing sports bra, choosing one made from Merino wool is surprisingly the move. “I don’t know about you, but when I thought ‘wool,’ the first thing that came to mind was an itchy winter sweater—not exactly what I’m going for when I’m shopping for a sports bra,” states fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT. But Branywyn’s Essential Busty Bra (and really everything we’ve tried from the brand) has been everything but itchy or uncomfortable.

Merino wool as a technical fabric has been a “revelation” for Grief, because it’s one of the few natural fibers that performs well in activewear. It comes from the coat of sheep and other animals, is naturally antimicrobial, and wicks away and absorbs sweat rather than letting it sit on the skin. If you run hot during your workouts, you can trust this bra to dry quickly and even wear it straight from the gym to brunch or errands if needed.

It has been revealed that grief indicates the bra doesn’t chafe or feel scratchy in any way, which is partially due to the fabric and partially due to the (nearly) seamless construction. The bottom band is a raw edge with no underwire, so it feels weightless and smooth, but also doesn’t ride up. It provides medium support, so it’s great for all workouts except HIIT classes. But it handles strength training, incline walks, casual jogs, and yoga or Pilates with ease.

You want to make sure your sports bra is made from high-quality, breathable fabrics, such as the ones below.

When looking for a sports bra, you should know the difference between compression and encapsulation in your bra. Compression, which can be found in the Nike or Lululemon sports bras, offers the feeling of your boobs being so supported that they’re a bit squished and pushed down. Encapsulation lifts, cradles, and separates your girls while still eliminating boob bounce. It can be found in the Beyond Yoga bra. In terms of support, there are three options to choose from when shopping:.

In a recent development, as Women's Health editors, we practically live in sports bras. Our editors and testers are of all different fitness levels, ages, and sizes. For this story, I spoke to style contributors Lily Wohlner, Rose Lauture, and Kristen Saladino, as well as executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, about their favorite sports bras for running, high-intensity training, low-intensity activity, and lounging. Then, we narrowed down our list and retested them at the gym. We rated them based on comfort, support, breathability, moisture-wicking abilities, and the list goes on. The options that got the highest marks are the ones that made it onto this list.

15 Airbnbs With Indoor Pools & Jacuzzis (2026): Top Summer Escapes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that airbnbs with indoor pools (especially the heated kind) are the kinds of “needle in a haystack” rentals that can save a vacation from feeling completely miserable in the coldest months of the year, or heighten the excitement of the enclave you’ve secured for a week of summer bliss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that airbnbs with indoor pools (especially the heated kind) are the kinds of “needle in a haystack” rentals that can save a vacation from feeling completely miserable in the coldest months of the year, or heighten the excitement of the enclave you’ve secured for a week of summer bliss. And though many of your standard Airbnb rentals will offer guests some generous amenities—a plush bed, a functional kitchen, and a high-pressure shower immediately come to mind—only a very select few allow you to book a pool that’s all yours (not shared, or fought over, by a bunch of resort guests). Better yet: There’s no “pool closes at 9 p.m.” signs.

But here’s the catch: The gap between a great indoor-pool rental and a truly tragic one is vast. We’re talking sleek, glass-wrapped sanctuaries on one end—and, on the other, a sad, chlorinated afterthought hiding in a basement with fluorescent lighting and 1994 motel energy. The good ones, though, have the power to allow you to lock in your vacation and tune everything else out. From a cedar-lined pool room with views of the surrounding forest to modern desert escapes where you can watch the sunset turn the surrounding mountains pink at sunset from your floaty, these pools make for an incredible retreat year-round, weather be damned.

Perks: Turkish steam bath, sauna, massage room, private chef, butler service, private backyard, security system.

If your ideal vacation involves frescoed ceilings, crystal chandeliers, and a butler to fetch you juice that’s been freshly squeezed from the garden's citrus trees, Villa Dorata in Positano delivers. This five-bedroom Baroque-style villa is gloriously over the top, with jewel-toned interiors, gilded art, elaborate tilework, and terraces overlooking the Amalfi Coast. The private spa is an attraction in its own right, complete with an indoor swimming pool, Turkish steam bath, and massage room. Outside, lush gardens, fountains, and citrus groves provide plenty of places to enjoy the Mediterranean sunshine. There are even two traditional Italian pizza ovens for alfresco dinners. Daily breakfast, housekeeping, and butler service are included, so guests can spend less time managing the logistics of a group vacation and more time enjoying the villa's considerable extravagance. From $5,078 per night.

Perks: Jetted bathtub, private backyard, fire pit, outdoor furniture, pet-friendly, security system, free parking.

In a recent development, swimming season never ends at this three-bedroom home outside Binghamton, Latest York. The heated indoor pool occupies its own glass-lined space, supplying views of the surrounding trees and simulating the feeling of being outdoors. The rest of the house features vaulted ceilings, bamboo floors, and a contemporary mix of furnishings. Floor-to-ceiling windows let in plenty of natural light into the main living areas, and an expansive deck extends the entertaining space outdoors. There's also a balcony for morning coffee, a propane fire pit for chilly evenings, and a jetted soaking tub in the primary suite. With room for eight guests and a pet-friendly policy, it's a practical choice for a group getaway, particularly when the weather makes an outdoor pool considerably less appealing. From $425 per night.

Perks: Soaking tub, sauna, two fireplaces, private deck.

The Catskills have no shortage of cabins with fireplaces and woodland views, but few come with their own indoor swimming pool. This four-bedroom getaway near Callicoon has all three, plus an infrared sauna for the ultimate wellness-centric stay. Cathedral ceilings, exposed timber, and two wood-burning fireplaces give the interiors a classic mountain house look, while oversized windows keep the surrounding three acres of forest in view. Outside, a path leads down to Callicoon Creek, and a generously-sized deck and fire pit make the most of the secluded setting. The house sleeps 10, so there's room to bring a crowd without having to share a hotel pool with strangers. From $410 per night.

Perks: Hot tub, spa deck, sun patio, grilling area, gourmet kitchen.

Industry observers note that there are indoor pools, and then there are homes built entirely around them. This sprawling five-bedroom retreat centers on a private heated mineral pool and hot tub housed in a dedicated spa space, turning a weekend getaway into something closer to a wellness retreat. Elsewhere, the home feels equal parts time capsule and thoughtful renovation. Original details—including a vintage intercom system, wood-clad ceilings, and dramatic stonework—sit alongside updated bathrooms and an eclectic mix of vintage and contemporary furnishings. Thoughtful extras—from a grand piano and art supplies to a gourmet kitchen and eight smart TVs—make it particularly appealing for multigenerational gatherings. From $945 per night.

Perks: Indoor fireplace, private patio, dedicated parking, game room, wine cellar.

According to recent reports, from the outside, this townhouse looks like a regular Denver-area home. Inside, however, it’s organized around one genuinely unexpected element: a full-size indoor pool set beneath a ceiling of skylights and surrounded by greenery. A fireplace just off the pool deck gives swimmers a place to warm up between dips (or flips off the diving board). The rest of the house is built for groups who plan to stay put. Exposed brick and wood-paneled walls give the interiors a grounded, slightly retro feel, while oversized bedrooms and bathrooms make it comfortable for longer stays rather than quick weekends. A wine cellar and wet bar sit near the pool room, clearly intended for nights that stretch on, and a separate game room—complete with a pool table and shuffleboard—adds another place to gather. From $726 per night.

Perks: BBQ, fire pit, heated indoor pool, washer and dryer.

The Invisible House, with its mirror-clad façade, is a well-known landmark in its area of the Joshua Tree Desert. Designed by architect Tomas Osinski, the home quite literally reflects its surroundings while an open plan setup connects one end of the space to the other—encompassing a lengthy 100-foot indoor pool, four bedrooms, and common areas dotted with modern furnishings from the likes of Piero Lissoni and Pierre Paulin. Staying here ensures a prime place for trekking out on hikes, while indoors you can take in wraparound views of the landscape while you swim laps in the deep end. From $2,333 per night.

Perks: Two game rooms, multiple smart TVs, fire pit, disc golf, covered balcony.

In a recent development, this Hot Springs hideaway is unapologetically built for groups who proposal to stay in. Set on four wooded acres behind a gated entry, the house revolves around a heated, salt-water indoor pool—kept at a reliably cozy 85 degrees. Four bedrooms (three with en-suite baths) comfortably sleep a crowd, while two dedicated game rooms—stocked with everything from billiards and karaoke to arcade games, air hockey, and ping-pong—give the house a choose-your-own-adventure feel. Outside, the acreage adds privacy and offers a fire pit and covered balcony for enjoying nature. From $822 per night.

Perks: Fireplace, breakfast nook, porch, farm animals.

According to recent reports, for a pastoral adventure with some thoroughly modern comforts, book this inn located on a farm 45 minutes out from Portland, Maine. Here, you’ll be occupying the cozy second floor suite, which offers a living room with a fireplace on cold winter nights and polished sleeping quarters. Since the inn sits on a working farm, you can also commune with the cute sheep and goats on the property, which spans 100 acres for walking and exploring the local fields. From $183 per night.

Perks: Game room, fireplaces, furnished deck, fire pit, movie projector.

It has been revealed that if your idea of a perfect mountain getaway involves never hearing the words "I'm bored," this Poconos rental has you covered. The four-bedroom home pairs a private heated indoor pool and spa with a long list of rainy-day diversions, including a dedicated game room stocked with foosball, ping-pong, shuffleboard, and a poker table, plus a media room with surround sound and an Xbox. Upstairs, the vibe is bright and contemporary, with an open-blueprint living area, two gas fireplaces, and a renovated kitchen anchored by an oversized dining table that seats 12. When the weather cooperates, the fun spills outdoors, where you'll find two furnished decks, a fire pit, and access to the community's lake, sports courts, and seasonal pools. From $900 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, electric car charger, laundry.

Colorado is a state known for its epic ski resorts and wintery locales, but in the city of Colorado Springs, all kinds of adventures await when you book this Southwestern-style home that feels all but plucked out of the desert. The jewel of the home is its long stretch of indoor pool that heats up to 90 degrees Fahrenheit so you can break a sweat even when it’s in the single digits outside. Spread across multiple levels that include plenty of terraces for enjoying the great outdoors, you can also get up and close and personal with nature on any of the surrounding hiking trails (including the ones that snake through Pulpit Rock Park and Garden of the Gods). From $755 per night.

According to recent reports, the biggest perk of this rustic five-bedroom chalet in Plymouth, Vermont, is its proximity to Okemo Mountain and the slopes of Killington Peak. But after a long day on the slopes, your aching limbs might need a cooldown, which is where the home’s sizable indoor pool comes in. Surrounded by stone walkways and a comfy seating area, plus accompanied by a wood-paneled sauna, the pool area offers several ways to unwind. Elsewhere, the cozy cabin invites you in with a stone fireplace and modern amenities like smart TVs and central heating. Large windows throughout the home also let you take in the stunning views of surrounding mountains as you lounge or share meals. From $1,685 per night.

Perks: Home gym, game room, mountain and desert views.

Sources indicate that this amazing home in Tucson’s Catalina Foothills features an indoor pool with a second-story walking track, a home gym, and an extensive game room that encourages some healthy competitiveness. Guests have access to the entire home, which consists of four bedrooms and seven bathrooms—so go ahead and invite everyone on the group chat. When (or if) you decide to venture out, you’ll find yourself in close proximity to several great hiking trails, shops, restaurants, and golf courses that let you practice your swing. From $885 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, fishing ponds, sauna.

The misleading name of the town aside, there’s nothing small about this property. In fact, with 13 bedrooms, two fishing ponds, and 33 acres of land to explore, you may not even need to venture off the property. With all that space, it’s hardly surprising that this classic sideboard farmhouse even thought to include an indoor pool. There’s also a sauna and hot tub on one side and a game room complete with a slate pool table, a stylish bar, and a card table on the other. From $2,695 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, hiking trails, pond.

This custom-built lodge is situated on 19 private acres of land in the mountains of Pennsylvania, with 5,400 feet of lush wilderness to admire—including a private pond—from the heated indoor pool, which sits on the lower level of a two-story loft space clad in warm cedar wood planks. There’s even a firepit. For anyone willing to brave the cold, the private pool area houses the largest of the home’s five decks and boasts tables with room for 12 along with a collection of Adirondack chairs. Though the snowcapped mountain landscapes are quite visible from just about any of the estate’s rooms—including the six bedrooms and great room with high ceilings and a fireplace—the views are best from this particular terrace. Otherwise, immerse yourself in the surrounding nature by taking to the hiking trails. From $1,491 per night.

Perks: Fireplace, hot tub, sauna.

According to recent reports, skiers and snowboarders headed to the rugged mountains of Substantial Sky can enjoy a special après ski experience by way of this 25,000-square-foot estate with a 60 foot heated indoor pool, hot tub, and sauna. After working up an appetite in the deep end, you can pop over to the chef’s kitchen and adjacent dining room (which features two dining tables that seat up to 12 people each) for a recovery meal. Or, for the more traditional chalet experience, sit back and relax in front of the floor-to-ceiling stone fireplace in the living room, which is the definition of rustic coziness thanks to its beamed ceilings and warm décor. From $7,062 per night.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, who notes long EV road trips mean hours at charging stations? BMW drove the latest i3 for over 3 days, covering nearly 3,700 miles, and it took less than 3 hours of charging.

BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.

Sources indicate that the Paneurpeana, as it’s called, is considered the benchmark for range and charging speed. The route begins at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe you can reach by car, and ends in Tarifa, Spain, the southernmost point of mainland Europe.

BMW drove the new i3 50 xDrive for a total of 3,658 miles (5,886.7 km) across eight countries and spent just 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds charging at an average of 275 kW.

The performance beat the previous record by more than seven hours, according to Mike Reichelt, head of BMW’s Neue Klasse.

BMW noted the charging points were not predetermined and that it had to account for external factors such as weather and traffic jams.

The newly introduced i3 was impressively efficient during the trip, consuming an average of just 12.5 kWh per 100 km, beating its official WLTP combined energy consumption of 18-13.4 kWh/100 km.

BMW said the trip took 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes, with an average speed of 79.7 km/h, and that the i3 was charged exclusively at public charging points across national charging networks.

The vehicle was driven at all times by a single driver and was not modified in any way, in terms of hardware or software, from the standard i3 available for purchase.

BMW’s latest i3 uses a 108.7 kWh battery and Gen6 eDrive system that provides a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

With a drag coefficient of just 0.21, the newly introduced i3 is the most aerodynamically efficient BMW vehicle to date.

In the US, BMW said the new 2027 i3 50 xDrive will offer an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 468 miles.

With an 800V architecture, the electric sedan can add nearly 262 miles (423 km) of range (WLTP) in about 10 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds up to 400 kW. In the US, the i3 has a built-in NACS port.

Very reasonable. I've been with NK iX3 from Spain to Estonia and the experience is real - low consumption, great comfort and really fast charging. And there are more and more high speed chargers every month.

Like the new iX3, the i3 features BMW’s Neue Klasse interior design. The setup consists of BMW’s massive 43″ Panoramic Vision display that spans the base of the windshield and a 17.9″ floating central infotainment display.

The fresh BMW i3 50 xDrive is on sale in Germany starting at €65,900 with a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

In the US, the 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive and 2027 iX3 50 xDrive are available to order, both starting at $61,500.

I’ve tested more bras than I can count as a style writer. And over the years, I’ve learned that comfort is a nonnegotiable—if it digs, pinches, or rides up, it doesn’t deserve a space in my drawer. The thing is, no two boobs are exactly alike (not even your own). One might sit higher, be fuller, or have a different shape than the other. So finding the right bra isn’t about hitting a standard size—it’s about understanding your body. According to Navya Mysore, MD, a primary care physician and Women’s Health advisor, the right bra boosts comfort, improves posture, and eases back pain by evenly distributing breast tissue. If your band rides up, your straps slide, or your underwire doesn’t lie flat, it’s a clear sign something’s off.

It has been revealed that and if your usual size suddenly stops working? Totally normal. Bra fitter and undergarment educator Kimmay Caldwell says weight changes, hormone shifts, or your monthly cycle can impact your size. To make it trickier, some brands still use outdated sizing methods (like the “plus four” rule), while others go by your exact underbust. Bottom line: your size can change and vary between clothing brands.

All of that can make bra shopping feel like a bit of a minefield, which is exactly why I tested 20 different styles across fits, fabrics, and support levels to find the ones that are actually worth your money. These ten passed the wear test and then some, proving that comfort, support, and style actually can exist in one bra.

Sources indicate that A bra should fit your body—not the other way around—and Knix totally got the memo with this one. It feels snug at first, but it softens and molds to your shape with every wear. What really impressed me was the fit because it almost feels custom, thanks to the ultra-thin foam that contours without adding volume.

Plus, the sleek fabric (a nylon-spandex blend) moves with you, feeling super smooth against the skin and breathable enough to wear for hours.

If you're after definition without the discomfort, this wire-free option def delivers. The molded cups lift and separate, while subtle side padding helps prevent spillage and sideboob. The result? A natural shape, no extra bulk, and no awkward lines under tighter tops. And with 99 sizes (!!) and eight colors, the options are actually inclusive.

In a recent development, the only downside? It’s not the best for high movement and workouts. I find myself adjusting it when I bend or move swiftly. Still, for everyday comfort and a super flattering fit, this one’s a standout.

It has been revealed that if you love the shape and support of a traditional bra but can't stand the feel of underwire, the Shapermint Essentials Sweetheart Wireless Contour Bra is your happy medium. It delivers a surprisingly lifted, rounded silhouette without a single wire digging into your ribs, making it my top pick for anyone who wants all-day comfort.

The lightly contoured foam cups provide just enough structure to prevent the dreaded uniboob, while the wide, stretchy band stays comfortably in place without pinching or rolling. The smooth, buttery fabric feels soft against the skin and disappears nicely under T-shirts and other fitted tops.

I was especially impressed by how supportive it feels for a wireless bra. It lifts and shapes without feeling restrictive, and the wider straps help distribute weight so your shoulders don't pay the price after hours of wear. It's one of those bras you forget you're wearing—which is pretty much the highest compliment I can give.

Recent findings suggest that push-up bras with underwires have a bad rep, and for good reason. They’re usually stiff, pokey, and downright uncomfortable. But after wearing this Maidenform bra for months (yes, months), I can confidently say it’s a major exception to the rule.

Sources indicate that from the start, this bra felt different. The underwire doesn’t dig or jab, thanks to its soft, stretchy crochet lace that moves with you. The cups are unpadded but still offer that ideal medium support and lift, enough to give shape and a gentle push-up effect, but never so much that I feel squeezed or overly sculpted. It’s supportive without being suffocating, which is rare in the world of push-ups.And let’s talk about the straps. They’re fully adjustable and convertible, so whether I’m going for a classic or criss-cross fit, I can tweak the style to match my outfit. That kind of versatility makes it feel like you’re getting two bras in one (and who doesn’t love a multitasker?).The lift it gives is subtle but effective. It’s not the dramatic “hello, cleavage” kind of push-up, but more of a natural, perky boost that works under everything from tees to low-cut dresses. No spillage, just a flattering shape that makes me feel more confident in whatever I’m wearing. Bonus points for the range of styles: It comes in smooth fabric options to wear under clingy tees, and lace versions for when you want to have a little more fun.One of my biggest bra fears? The dreaded back and side bulge. But this bra’s smoothing side panels genuinely help—there’s no weird digging or over-compression, just a smooth, flattering fit that doesn’t fight with your body. Long story short: I tested it, I lived in it, and I’m keeping it in my regular rotation.

As someone who hates wearing bras (the wires, the bulk, the digging), this is the one I wear most. Made for fuller busts (DD+), the Cosabella Evolution Curvy Bralette lifts and shapes with lightly molded cups, no wires necessary.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s the only bralette I’ve found that can actually support my chest without feeling restrictive,” claims style contributor Lily Wohlner. The soft, stretchy fabric, made from a smooth microfiber that consists of 85 percent polyamide and 15 percent elastane, molds to your body, starting snug and swiftly adapting for a custom-like fit. “I will say, mine have stretched a bit over the past few years, so it might be time to re-up,” she says.

Sources indicate that this bra provides exceptional support for larger busts, even without a heavy-duty wire band. Instead, it makes use of an elasticized band that provides a surprisingly large amount of support without digging into the skin. It also has extra support at the sides to prevent spillage and to keep everything looking seamless, even under thin t-shirts and tight dresses.

The adjustable straps and underband stay put, and the side coverage smooths everything out—no spillage, no weird lines under shirts. It gives a natural, rounded shape that works under pretty much anything.

According to recent reports, if you tend to scoop the girls into place to make them look perkier (a good trick!), this Cuup bra does the work for you. The rounded neckline and unlined, unpadded cups naturally lift and shape, while seamlessly extending into the straps for clean lines and a flattering fit.

It runs snug, but that’s what makes it so supportive—my boobs stay put and look perkier without any adjusting. The underwire is super lightweight and flexible, so there’s zero digging or poking there. I also love that the cups are unlined, because it makes the bra feel super lightweight and barely there.

Recent findings suggest that the bra is made from a microfiber blend of polyamide and elastane, so it’s buttery-smooth, stretches with you while keeping its shape, and is ultra-breathable. It’s great for warm days since it feels like next to nothing on the skin and helps wick moisture away. The microfiber is also great for pairing with thin or tight tops, since it's basically undetectable under clothing—no lines in sight.

The straps are fully adjustable for a customizable lift, and even though the cups are thin, they still offer enough coverage to prevent any chilly-day surprises, IYKYK. Since the cups run a bit small, sizing up might be your best bet for full coverage.

The Honeylove CrossOver Bra is ultra-comfortable, smoothing, and supportive. The nylon and spandex blend feels soft and wearable for hours without digging into your skin while providing a completely seamless silhouette from every angle. I always wear this pick under thinner tops, tight dresses, and clingy sweaters because it creates a totally streamlined look under clothes while lifting the girls and supporting the underarm area and sides.

Sources indicate that plus, the bonded cradle under the bust mimics the structure of an underwire, delivering firm support without any poking or pinching. The full mesh overlay adds light compression and lift, adding to the sleek look.

According to recent reports, “The CrossOver bra feels like a sports bra on, which is especially handy for women in search of something extra-comfortable (hi),” says contributor Korin Miller, who wore this bra every day for nearly a month to see how well it performed. She appreciates the flexible boning at the sides of the cups to prevent sideboob and bulging.

This bra also has one of the widest size ranges on our list, which is a major win. However, it does run a little big, so if you're between sizes, consider sizing down for the best fit.

In a recent development, finding a lace bra that's actually comfortable—especially if you have a larger bust—can feel like a tall order, but the Bravissimo Millie Bra proves you don't have to sacrifice support for something pretty. It's my top pick for fuller busts thanks to its soft stretch lace cups, which mold to your shape for a flexible, barely-there feel instead of digging in or gaping.

It has been revealed that unlike stiff, scratchy lace bras, this one feels surprisingly comfortable from the first wear. The unpadded cups hug your breasts without adding bulk, while the stretchy lace adapts to your natural shape for a fit that feels supportive without being restrictive. The delicate floral lace also gives it an elevated, feminine look that's pretty enough to show off under a slightly unbuttoned blouse or low-cut top.

Meanwhile, the side sling creates a naturally lifted, forward shape, and if you wear a JJ or K cup, those sizes include additional lining for even more support where you need it most. The result is a flattering silhouette that feels secure without relying on heavy padding.

Recent findings suggest that the Natori Bliss Perfection Bra nails the perfect balance of comfort and structure. It feels light and flexible but keeps everything perfectly lifted and in place. No readjusting is needed halfway through the day, as is so often the case. That's thanks to the stretchy fabric, fully adjustable straps and band, and the strong yet plush underwire.

It has been revealed that the smooth microfiber fabric (a nylon and spandex blend) feels buttery-soft against the skin, with just enough stretch to move as you do. Even the lace trim—sometimes a red flag for irritation—is whisper-smooth and lies flat under clothes. And while there’s an underwire, it’s so well-cushioned that it supports without poking or digging.

Industry observers note that it’s the only underwire bra I don’t rip off the second I get home. It’s really the only bra I reach for when I head to the office or if I’m wearing a top that requires a little more lift and support for that flattering look. Style-wise, it looks as good as it feels. The lightly-lined cups create a natural, rounded shape that disappears under everything from fitted tees to silk blouses, and the smooth band keeps the silhouette seamless.

According to recent reports, our only con? It’s handwash only. I tried washing mine in a mesh laundry bag the first time it needed a clean, and while it wasn’t destroyed, it definitely pilled a bit.

Sources indicate that if you have a smaller bust, you don't need a ton of padding to get a flattering fit—and the Journelle Victory Plunge Bra is proof. It's my top pick for A- to C-cups thanks to its lightly structured, unlined design that hugs your natural shape while disappearing under clothes.

According to recent reports, the contoured cups mold to your body for a smooth, comfortable fit, and because they lie completely flat, there's no bunching or gaping to contend with. Recent findings suggest that if you love a deep V-neckline but hate when your bra peeks out, meet your fresh go-to: the Harper Wilde Bliss Triangle Bralette. It’s become my go-to for daily wear, and the super-soft, barely-there material is truly the next best thing to going bra-free. Recent findings suggest that even without padding, the double-layered fabric gives solid nipple coverage. It comes in inclusive sizes and neutral shades that go with everything. The few cons? In a recent development, the most comfortable bras usually come down to the right blend of fabrics. Here’s what each one brings to the table:.

Recent findings suggest that comfort is about more than just size—it’s also about ensuring the wire doesn’t create pressure points or cause discomfort throughout the day. Look for bras with flexible, padded, or cushioned underwires, which offer support without digging into your skin. The underwire should sit flat against your ribcage and follow the natural curve of your breasts. If it feels like it’s poking or shifting, it’s not the right fit. If you prefer a wire-free bra, opt for styles with flexible boning, molded cups, and wide, flexible bands to provide support.

Recent findings suggest that the most accurate way to find your size is to get fitted in person. Once you have your size, your upcoming bra should feel snug and secure. The band should be comfortably tight, but not dig into the skin. A good rule of thumb is that you should be able to fit two fingers between the band and your skin, but no more. The cups should also lie flat against your chest.

According to recent reports, the Women’s Health team has been testing bras since we first wrote this story in 2023. To find the most comfortable options, our team wore each style for at least a few weeks at a time. We wore them under different circumstances, including workouts, lounging, and long days at the office. But our main criterion for each bra was comfort. I also spoke with two bra experts and personally tested 20-plus bras over several years to lock down the ones I actually wear on repeat.

Industry observers note that I recently re-tested a bunch of options and tapped style contributor Lily Wohlner for an upgrade to this story to boost our list and keep it up-to-date. The final guide includes everything from bralettes and seamless bras to push-up bras—and I actually wear all of them in my day-to-day life.

#29259. Breaking: Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

📅 16 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1039 w)
